source: Thumbs-down Radar P0/P1 findings on a production monorepo, adjudicated against the code and anonymised. None held at P0/P1.

cases.title: Concurrent index build runs under the startup probe and is missing from the out-of-band apply plan
cases.impact: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY must scan the whole table, which on a large cluster can exceed the startup probe; the container is then killed mid-migration while holding the migration lock.
cases.recommendation: Include the index in the out-of-band pre-apply for large environments, and add a lock-clear step to the interrupted-migration runbook.
cases.adjudication: partly right, severity wrong: the deploy plan did miss the index (the author added it), but the new column is stored out of line, so the build is cheap.
cases.note: Fixed by a guidance file next to the migrations, which Radar loads for migration files, not by the prompt.

cases.title: The backfill's per-batch COMMIT inside a DO block can fail on re-run under the migration runner's connection state
cases.impact: The runner's no-transaction mode protects the normal path, but any runner that wraps the file in BEGIN (or a future migration tool change) turns this into an immediate ERROR: COMMIT is not allowed in a DO block.
cases.recommendation: This is acceptable as shipped if verified against the actual runner (the migration test does exercise it), but add a defensive comment or assert autocommit at the top of the block.
cases.adjudication: false positive: the changeset runs in autocommit, and a migration test runs it through the real runner twice. The finding concedes it is acceptable as shipped and needs a hypothetical runner to fail.

cases.title: Enforce resource permissions before exposing bulk import
cases.impact: The newly exposed bulk-write path calls an endpoint gated only by a create permission, so a caller with create and list permissions can create bundled resources their role denies.
cases.recommendation: Authorize every bundled resource operation in the API service before any writes.
cases.adjudication: facts right, attribution and severity wrong: the endpoint's permission check is pre-existing and by design, the pull request does not change the API service, and the tool calls it with the caller's token, so it grants no new privilege. A product-security question for an owner, not a P0.

cases.title: Cutover silently stops batching for tenants carried by the retired flags
cases.impact: A tenant enabled on the old flags reverts to the code defaults with no warning, no metric and no error; the only verification is a manual log check.
cases.recommendation: Add a one-release warning or gauge at config read time, or gate the old-flag removal behind a second pull request.
cases.adjudication: right, author accepted the risk: no automated detection exists, but the runbook already documents the manual check and few tenants are affected.
cases.note: Not addressed: an operational-runbook risk with a documented manual check was proposed as P2 in the adjudication, but that rule was not approved for this change.

cases.title: No test checks lifecycle stop ordering in the wired applications
cases.impact: The flush guarantee depends on each application registering the fallback, then the producers, then every sender, in that order. A later refactor that moves a sender's registration earlier would silently drop buffered records again, and no test would fail.
cases.recommendation: Add a small test per service, or a shared helper test, that asserts the producers and the fallback come before the producing managed objects in the lifecycle.
cases.note: First raised in round 3 of 5 on lines the push had not changed. The ordering is correct as shipped; it fails only after a hypothetical later refactor, and the fix is a test, which the rubric rates P2.

boundary_cases.source: Radar's own review: a changed caller can introduce a risk through unchanged code
boundary_cases.example: The diff adds a handler that passes a request parameter to an existing runShell(cmd) helper the diff does not touch.
boundary_cases.why: The changed line newly exposes the existing sink to attacker input, so the risk is introduced even though the vulnerable helper is unchanged.

boundary_cases.source: Radar's own review: dormant newly added code keeps its severity
boundary_cases.example: The diff adds an exported ParseConfig that panics on an empty map; nothing calls it yet.
boundary_cases.why: The defect is in code this change adds; a future caller only triggers it, so the concession cap does not apply.
